THE SHANGHAI SUNDAY TIMES, FEBRUARY 9, 1930.

MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS

AS the end of the Municipal year approaches, residents in the International Settlement are beginning to speculate on the composition of the new Council. It is understood that there will be five Chinese Councillors and nine foreigners this year, each community selecting its own representatives. Although in certain Chinese circles there remains a feeling that two additional Chinese Councillors this year are inadequate, the majority of Chinese residents evince little interest in the matter. Unfortunately, there seldom has been serious competition for the foreign seats, and if rumour is correct this year there will be fewer experienced candidates than ever for the thankless task of administering the affairs of the Settlement. In spite of the addition to the Council staff of a Director-General and the bringing to Shanghai of Mr. Justice Feetham and at least one other as advisors, business men find the work of running this municipality altogether too great a tax on their time in these distressful days, and it is understood that even more persuasion than usual will need to be used to induce representative men to serve.

Meanwhile, the Chinese are again considering what it is they want of the Municipal Council above and beyond the unique advantages already enjoyed by residence in this area. We think it is a healthy sign that one of the first things the Chinese wish to get is a greater measure of public education for their children. Years ago the Council felt compelled to lay down the broad principles of its education policy, but the Chinese have never ceased to argue that it is the duty of the Council to provide a sufficient number of schools to meet the demand of the Chinese population, especially the working classes, for education. They fully understand that it would take years to build up a system of this nature, and that it would cost a large sum of money annually, but they are undaunted, arguing that the Chinese contribute most of the Municipal revenue and that a far greater sum is spent on the education of foreign children in Municipal schools than on Chinese. We think the Chinese should be encouraged in this ambition to secure education for the people in the various stations of life and at a price to suit their respective pockets. But obviously it is quite out of the question to achieve this purpose immediately: the Chinese criticism, of course, is that the Municipal schools are crowded and no attempt is being made by the Municipality to provide for the children of humbler folk. In this connection there is one point the Chinese nearly always overlook and it is that few educated foreigners find the educational facilities afforded in Shanghai adequate for their children, hence every spring there is an exodus of foreign children to the homelands, where they are left by parents compelled to return to Shanghai to earn their livelihood.

Another grievance of the Chinese is that the best-equipped hospitals are not available to them, except in very limited numbers and at charges which only the comparatively well-to-do can meet. This is a matter upon which the Chinese can have little to say with any degree of justification. There are large and extremely well-run hospitals in Shanghai provided solely for Chinese patients, both by missionary societies and by Chinese. Compared with the population these are insufficient; but it must be remembered that the percentage of Chinese who will go to a modern hospital is extremely small. As for the foreign community, it has no Municipal hospital for other than infectious cases, now that the Victoria Nursing Home has been closed to the public, and the Country Hospital has been so crowded of late that it has sometimes been impossible to secure a bed: and although the charges there are high enough, a police of cheeseparing appears to be followed, which surely would drive patients elsewhere if there were an alternative. The Chinese, therefore, certainly have no reason to complain that foreigners, who are accustomed to enter hospitals when overtaken by serious sickness, whereas Chinese are not, have any advantage over them.

Next comes the great question of giving Chinese more posts under the Municipal Council. Not unnaturally there is a demand among educated and partly-educated Chinese for employment where salaries are good and regularly paid. But it would seem they do not yet understand that the Municipal Council does not create posts in order to give employment at handsome salaries, and that the beginning already made to place Chinese in positions hitherto held by foreigners promises well for the future if a little patience is exercised.

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, TUESDAY, FEBRUARY 25, 1930

NOMINATIONS FOR
THE COUNCIL

The fact that fourteen nominations for the new Council have been received is an extremely healthy sign. It is the more important, in that this number has been attained with a minimum of previous publicity. A week ago it seemed as if there might be no election at all. Very few "letters to the Editor" have appeared. There has been no press campaign. But ratepayers have evidently thought things over for themselves and acted. One is reminded of the vote at the meeting of 1921 on the Salaries Commission's report: practically no indication of public feeling had been given in advance, but, without any speech in opposition to the report, it was thrown out by an overwhelming majority. In the present instance it is known that in some official quarters the view is held that it would be better not to have an election this year. Plainly that is not the ratepayers' view and certainly it is not ours. A very notable feature of the nominations is the wide range of interests they represent, indicating a general appreciation of the importance of the Council's duties, never indeed so conspicuous as to-day. So far from the public being apathetic towards municipal affairs, they are sincerely interested in them. With proper encouragement and by taking ratepayers more frequently into their confidence, the Council might find in this interest a weapon of the greatest service in the battles they have to fight.

To speak plainly, we believe there is a widespread feeling that the Council needs new blood and a more determined attitude. There appears too great a tendency to compromise and smooth things over, which merely means more ground lost; too much dread of "incidents," the surest possible way to provoke them; and too great a willingness to follow meekly where diplomatists lead, regardless of whether they have either the right or the intelligence to point the way. The secret meetings between Mr. Arnhold and Mr. Fessenden and the foreign delegates to the Provisional Court conference have made a deep and unfavourable impression on the public. We are anxious not to be unfair to the Chairman and Director-General who doubtless acted from the best motives. But while it does not yet appear that the Council knew of what they were doing, the regrettable result was that the Ministers concerned were enabled to telegraph to their respective Governments that representatives of the community had been consulted and, inferentially, had acquiesced in an agreement which, from the standpoint of Shanghai's interests, could scarcely be worse, and to which it is an open secret the delegates who were supposed to have negotiated it acceded under duress from their superiors. Here are matters on which the new nominees for the Council may well ponder. But most urgent is it that the present Council should take account of them without delay in order as far as possible to save the situation. We make no apology for returning to this most vital question. In plain English the Council and the foreign community have been "let down," where no such surrender was called for, by the men who should have been most concerned to defend their interests. But there are a few rights and safeguards of which the Council can avail themselves, if they set to work at once to decide what they will do and if they make it clear to the diplomatists that they will not allow their rights and authority to be further whittled away and undermined.

Part of the badness of the new Court agreement is that no one can decide precisely how it is to operate. We do not say that without reason. Persons who are more concerned in its working than any others have professed themselves uncertain as to its meaning. For example, how will it affect the Council's power of patrolling municipal roads outside Settlement limits? What will be the position of the waterworks, gas and electricity undertakings in respect of mains, pipes and cables which they have already laid on those roads and of which extensions will be needed in future? From one part of the agreement it would appear that all these important interests have been recklessly jettisoned; from another, that they may still be saved. This question is bound up with a further matter of great moment. Not quite two months ago Judge Feetham was brought out here to advise on the future constitution of Shanghai. His appointment is not due to any foreign Government, which indeed could not have recommended it. But it is well known that both the British and American Governments have bestowed an unofficial benediction on Judge Feetham's engagement and have expressed a lively interest in what he has to do. Why, then, have the diplomatists in China done their best to cut the ground from under his feet? For both the "outside" roads and other matters affected by the new agreement are an integral part of the whole problem on which Judge Feetham has to advise.

But the vagueness of the agreement tells both ways, enabling the Council to take a definite stand on certain points, which it would be hard for anyone to prove wrong and which nobody would resist in act, provided the Council make it quite clear that they mean what they say and will not be frightened or bamboozled into surrendering rights that are absolutely indispensable to their efficiency as the responsible Government of Shanghai. Thus, under the new agreement the Chinese Courts will take "due account" of the Land Regulations, which give the Council full powers over outside roads until the contrary has definitely been proved. Similarly, the right to lay water pipes and gas mains on outside roads would appear to follow the Land Regulations and is upheld by the custom of many years. In these and cognate questions the Council, being an international body, are under no obligation to study the susceptibilities of any particular Minister, and the extent to which they listen to representations from outside must be strictly subordinated to their duties as the one authority that has to bear the burden of the peace and welfare of Shanghai. As for the bugbear of "incidents" the one sure thing is that these rarely, if ever, occur in face of a resolute demeanour. Take the recent case of the gates on North Szechuen Road Extension, over which the local Chinese officials seemed so threatening. The Council stood firm, the gates were put up, and the threats came to nothing. Under the new Court agreement the Council can still assert themselves if they act promptly. But speed and resolution are indispensable. This the foreign community fully understand and they will not hold the Council guiltless if, in these few precious days that remain, there is vacillation and delay.

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 28, 1930.

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 28, 1930.

What The Candidates Say

In order to clarify the issues at the Municipal Council election, which will be held next Monday and Tuesday, "The Shanghai Times" has requested the candidates to give short but considered statements of their policies for the benefit of the electors. A selection is printed below, and others will be published as received.
...

MR. H. E. ARNHOLD:
In submitting my name for re-election this year, I can only once more emphasize that the Council's general policy must be to continue to work for efficiency, economy, and for the maintenance of the authority of the Council in the face of the continued attempts to undermine the same. The above policy has been followed consistently, and during the past year the recommendations of the Economy Committee have been carried out as far as was possible.
A Salaries Committee was appointed during the year and is still sitting to examine into the question of staff re-organization; the services of a highly qualified senior officer were secured as Commissioner of Police, with the kind assistance of the Indian Government, to investigate into the conditions of our Police Force, and to reorganize the same; our school system, both foreign and Chinese, is being overhauled, and despite all statements to the contrary, the authority of the Council has been maintained and its rights defended without exception.
The Council has consistently worked for a better understanding and for closer co-operation between the Foreign and Chinese ratepayers. It is only by establishing a friendly atmosphere with our Chinese fellow ratepayers and by co-operation with the same, that the Council can steer clear of the rocks which are ahead. The problems which face the Council are many and difficult, and it is in the hopes of finding a solution for the same that Judge Feetham has been appointed. The reason for this appointment have been fully explained in the press, and are endorsed by me.
The problem of the unsatisfactory telephone service has had the careful attention of the Council, who got out an expert from the British Post Office to give advice. It is hoped that this very difficult problem will be brought to a satisfactory solution shortly.
...

MR. NORMAN LESLIE:
If I am elected to the Council, it will be my endeavour to support all measures aiming at the maintenance of law and order within the Settlement, to secure the fullest protection for the legitimate interests of all sections of the community, and to promote friendly co-operation with our neighbours on lines calculated to further the best interests of Shanghai as a whole.
I am also in favour of as much publicity in matters affecting the Settlement as may be compatible with the Council's paramount duty to maintain law and order and with economy and efficiency in administration. I have had no previous experience of municipal work in Shanghai and am therefore unable to do more than present this outline of my general attitude.

MR. N. S. BROWN:
Although I am not disposed at this time to outline any particular views regarding the forthcoming Municipal election, I am prepared to state that my policy, if elected to the Council his year, will be to
[图片: Mr. N. S. Brown]
Mr. N. S. BROWN
do my utmost to prevent anything happening in the conduct of municipal affairs which might impede or restrict in any way the investigations now being made by Mr. Justice Feetham on behalf of the Council.
So much depends on the publication of Mr. Feetham's report that any statement I might make upon policy at this time would, I think, be out of place. Whatever the result of the election may be, I hope that every effort will be made to see that nothing untoward is likely to occur while Mr. Feetham is engaged in his responsible and delicate task.
...

MR. P. W. MASSEY:
Having been a member of he Council whose year of office is now coming to an end I fully subscribe to the policy it has followed. The appointment of Judge Feetham will, in my opinion, stand out in local history as the most constructive act of the year towards the goal of arriving at a permanent constitution for this settlement mutually satisfactory to Chinese and foreign interests.
Whilst the immediate future presents no particular question of burning interest, undoubtedly the Government of this Settlement will continue to be faced with weighty
(Continued on Page 2, Col. 5.)

problems, the solution of which will constitute a great responsibility.
The recent strengthening of the Police Force and the re-organization of its working should do much to suppress crime and I consider the vigorous support of this policy of prime importance.
I am of opinion that a more forward programme of public works such as widening of main arteries, extension of sewerage system etc., should be adopted now that financial conditions are easier than they were. The scientific disposal of refuse is a problem which is now receiving urgent attention and no efforts should be spared towards achieving complete independence in this respect.
Whilst the telephone service is not a Municipal undertaking but is in the hands of a public company, I consider that it is the paramount duty of the Council to do all in its power to ensure a really satisfactory service to subscribers and this has been the policy of the Council now in office.
Economy in the working of the Municipal administration should be sought by the more extensive employment of Chinese and the gradual reduction of imported labour which at the present exchange must constitute an increasingly heavy burden.

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 28, 1930.
（印：C. I. D. REGISTRY No. I. O. D. 1043 Date... 7 - 3 - 30）

AN ELECTION ADDRESS
To the Editor of the
"NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS."
SIR,—By your courtesy I have the honour to present to the Ratepayers a short report on my work in the Council during the current Municipal Year.
The Standing Committees of which I am a member are those dealing with "Works," with "Finance," with "Public Utilities" and with "Chinese Education." The routine work of these Committees has been on the whole, by the help of a very efficient permanent staff, smoothly and satisfactorily done. The problem of Refuse Disposal has given cause for anxiety to the members of the Works Committee and there have been occasional difficulties about the outside roads. On the whole, however, this Committee can look back upon a year of progress and forward to a period of still quicker development. The improved financial position of the Municipality has not led the Finance Committee into suggesting extravagance, but it is no longer necessary to postpone desirable public improvements on the sole ground of inability to afford the expense. The Public Utilities Committee has had under consideration during the year the franchises or tariffs of the Waterworks Company, the Omnibus Company, the Tram Company and the Telephone Company. I was till lately the nominee of the Council on the board of the last named Company but my relations with the chairman of the Council in that connection left so much to be desired that I have resigned that position (becoming at the same time an ordinary director of the Company) in the hope that better progress may be made through a more tactful liaison officer. My programme of action in connection with the Telephone Company is unchanged: I advocate the immediate sale of the Company along the lines laid down by the expert appointed by the Council. It was only after ceasing to represent the Council on the Telephone Board that I joined the Chinese Education Committee and I have thus too short an experience of its work to be able to comment on it.
In the debates at Council meetings I have taken an active, perhaps a too active, part. I have sat in six successive Councils and have been more and oftener acrimonious at the meetings of the present Council than at those of the preceding five added together. From my point of view this acrimony was usually caused by a discovery or a suspicion of things being done or attempted in the name of the Council without my knowledge or consent. A Coun-

cillor cannot be expected to accept responsibility for proceedings about which he could and should have been consulted, but was not.
In writing this report, which I do without ill-will to anyone, I am influenced by the opinion that there is much needless secrecy about Municipal affairs and that electors are entitled to know a great deal more than they do about the way in which the men whom they put into office enable the duties and opportunities entrusted to them. I am sure that the admission of Press and public to the meetings of Council, under proper safeguards, would be advantageous both to the community in general and to the Councillors themselves.
I am, etc.,
A. D. BELL.
Shanghai, Feb. 27, 1930.

THE SHANGHAI SUNDAY TIMES, MARCH 2, 1930.

THE MUNICIPAL ELECTION
THE Municipal Election to-morrow and Tuesday was robbed of some of its interest by the withdrawal of the first woman candidate to be proposed; and it was anticipated that the “straw vote” of the American community upon the three remaining candidates of that nationality would reduce the contest to a fight among the eight Britons. But at the time of writing the position is that the American community officially supports Mr. J. W. Carney and the Rev. C. E. Patton, while Mr. G. E. Tucker is also continuing his candidature. It has become a recognized practice to elect five Britons to the Council, two Americans and two Japanese, so that the nations having the largest interests in the welfare of the Foreign Settlement shall each be adequately represented. The two Japanese, who can command about 600 votes from their nationals, are practically certain of election, and it is believed by some that of the three Americans Mr. Tucker is most likely not to succeed, as a result of Friday’s meeting; Mr. Tucker, however, is confident of success. In addition to the five retiring British Councillors—H. E. Arnhold (Chairman), Brig.-General E. B. Macnaghten, Messrs. P. W. Massey, G. W. Sheppard and A. D. Bell—, Messrs. A. J. Hughes, N. S. Brown and N. Leslie have been nominated. Of the three new candidates, Mr. Hughes has unsuccessfully contested a previous election. He has been identified with local affairs for many years, especially with the now defunct Ratepayers’ Association. Messrs. Brown and Leslie are nominated for the first time. As business men who represent large interests, they stand primarily for law and order and the protection of the interests of all sections of the community. Mr. Brown also declares that he will do his utmost to prevent anything in the conduct of Municipal affairs which may impede or restrict Mr. Justice Feetham’s investigations. It will not be easy for voters to choose between the British candidates.

Of the two Japanese nominees, Mr. K. Fukushima has been a Councillor for three years, and has always been a valued member of the administration. Mr. T. Saito is one of the leading members of the Japanese community, being the General Manager of the N.Y.K. Line, and is proposed by Mr. T. Funatsu, Chairman of the Japanese Cotton Millowners’ Association, who is retiring on account of pressure of business. Both Mr. J. W. Carney and the Rev. C. E. Patton to-day state their views publicly for the first time. As candidates of the American community they may expect to poll a large number of votes. Mr. Tucker’s announced intention to preserve to the utmost degree the integrity of local laws and privileges and to resist attempts to have them chipped away, should win him votes, while his record on the Traffic Committee and the fact that he was partly responsible for keeping trams off Avenue Edward VII, for the development of that important thoroughfare and for the widening of Nanking Road, will be remembered.

In looking over the statements made by candidates as to their policies we find great stress laid upon the maintenance of law and order, on municipal economy, closer co-operation between Chinese and foreigners, upon the importance of Mr. Justice Feetham’s investigation and report, and upon the need of greater publicity in regard to Municipal affairs, with Mr. A. D. Bell coming out strongly as an advocate of a progressive policy in public works development. Mr. Sheppard stands, among other things, for the widest possible measures to prevent the commission of major crime, while his suggestion that the east and west traffic problem can be solved by culverting the Soochow Creek from the Bund to Markham Road and constructing a canal from Markham Road to the Point appeals to the imagination. Similarly, Mr. Fukushima’s declaration that any change in the status of Shanghai must receive the most careful consideration of foreign and Chinese interests involved should gain him votes outside his own community. Mr. Arnhold stands for efficiency, economy, the maintenance of authority, with closer Sino-foreign co-operation; while Mr. Massey looks for a permanent constitution mutually satisfactory to Chinese and foreigners as a result of Judge Feetham’s work here. He would also employ more Chinese in Municipal staffs, thereby effecting economy. General Macnaghten believes in closer co-operation with the Chinese, strict economy, and safeguarding the community’s interests. He has a record of service that should ensure his return. The result of the poll is awaited with unusual interest.

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, TUESDAY, MARCH 4, 1930.

Editor,
THE SHANGHAI TIMES
Sir,—With reference to the admirable letter signed "British Ratepayer" which appeared in a contemporary on March 2 and in view of the almost insuperable difficulty, for ratepayers who do not represent large financial interests, of ascertaining in any detail the records and opinions of the candidates for election to the Council, it has been suggested to me by certain friends that, by way of a change from the subterranean methods subsequently employed at elections of various kinds in Shanghai, I should ventilate for consideration and discussion some views, with all of which I agree, and with some of which I understand numerous other ratepayers agree.
In the first place in connection with the aldermanic election I see that Mr. H. E. Arnold seconded Mr. Saito, Mr. N. S. Brown was seconded by Mr. Fukashima, and that Brig.-General Macnaghten seconded Mr. Fukashima. Now it is hoped that those Japanese electors who are unacquainted with the respective merits of the British candidates will abstain from voting blindly as a body for these or any other British candidates, so that British and other electors with their possibly slightly fuller knowledge of the merits and qualifications of the British candidates may select those whom they prefer.
Points For Electors
In spite of the almost impenetrable veil of secrecy with which the Council or some of its members, for reasons which are unintelligible to the ordinary man, appear to desire to clothe not only their deliberations but also in some cases their intentions until they are accomplished facts, there are a few points concerning some of the candidates which are known to certain electors; but there are other points with regard to which a not wholly illegitimate curiosity still exists.
Taking the British candidates in their order of nomination the following are some of the more important facts which have obtruded themselves upon certain ratepayers, including myself, who have no personal or other interest in the election except to see, what we consider to be, the best British candidates, elected at a time like the present.
1.—Mr. H. E. Arnold.
(a) There is understood to be a fairly widespread feeling that he should not be elected, and, that if he is elected, he should not be re-elected Chairman.
(b) Among other reasons for voting against him are briefly his general record as Chairman, which does not inspire confidence and the facts disclosed in Mr. A. D. Bell's letter which appeared in the issue of the "North China Daily News" of February 28.

2.—Mr. A. D. Bell.
His letter referred to above is courageous, balanced and unambiguous and he is undoubtedly worthy of election.
3.—Mr. N. S. Brown.
Has told us comparatively little about his views; but if his statement that his policy will be "to do his utmost to prevent anything happening in the conduct of Municipal affairs which might impede or restrict in any way the investigations now being made by Mr. Justice Feetham on behalf of the Council" means that he is prepared to an immediate increase of Chinese Councillors until the issue of Mr. Justice Feetham's report, he is acceptable as a candidate.
4.—Mr. A. J. Hughes.
His stand for more publicity, his former services in civic matters and the desirability for new blood on the Council make him an acceptable candidate.
5.—Mr. Norman Leslie.
His statement of policy, his position, his reputation and the desirability of new blood on the Council make him an acceptable candidate.
6.—Brig.-General E. B. Macnaghten.
His general views and his record are eminently acceptable but his statement: "I am in favour of immediately increasing the number of Chinese representatives on the Council to five" is difficult to reconcile with his other statement "We should however, insist on the status quo being maintained pending any further decisions as a result of Judge Feetham's report." Why get Mr. Justice Feetham out here and then start tinkering with the constitution before he has been out here three months?
In the interests also of Chinese and foreigners alike why not wait until Mr. Justice Feetham or the Chinese or some one else has devised a Chinese electoral system, so that not only Chinese but foreigners may know what the views of Chinese candidates are on a variety of topics and so that the ratepayers generally both Chinese and foreign many have some guarantee, remote though it may be, that Chinese Councillors represent even roughly the views of Chinese ratepayers and not those of some other body or bodies.
Brig.-General Macnaghten's precipitancy in this connection causes us alarm and to our great regret we cannot support him for this reason on this occasion.
7.—Mr. P. W. Massey.
Although apparently in other respects eminently acceptable, his objection to greater publicity, particularly at a time like the present, is in the view of many a fatal objection to his candidature.

8.—Mr. G. W. Sheppard.
Is singularly reticent and non-committal in his views except with regard to the fact that he appears to consider with advancing years that it might have increased his present peace of mind if at an earlier stage in his career he had adopted the Church as a profession. He has, however, perhaps failed to realise that to a certain extent his reputed connection with the Church may possibly have contributed to a certain extent to the fact that he has enjoyed during the preceding year those mundane honours which fall to the lot of a Councillor; and in any event, it is surely never too late for him to embark upon the career to which his inclinations and maturer wisdom now call him. It is difficult for any human being not gifted with a superhuman prescience to foretell from his election address how he will act in certain circumstances. Apart; however, from this ordinarily becoming modesty and reserve he is generally considered politically sound and is therefore an acceptable candidate.
From the above observations it will be seen that the present intention of certain ratepayers, including myself, at the moment of writing is to vote for the British Candidates as follows:—
1. Mr. A. D. BELL
2. Mr. N. LESLIE
3. Mr. G. W. SHEPPARD
4. Mr. A. J. HUGHES

reflections. In the first place
the delegates told him that their

Machiavellian designs to the

sult of these secret meetings
was to put them in the position

PROVISIONAL COURT
To the Editor of the
"NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS."
SIR,—In your issue of the 8th instant I am reported to have stated that the Council had not been given an opportunity to consider the draft agreement, but that Mr. Fessenden and myself had been consulted, which amounted to the same thing as the Council taking part in the negotiations.
I attach copy of a letter which I wrote to you at the time, but which I did not forward, as, on reconsideration, the statement of your reporter was, on the face of it, so absurd that it did not seem to me to require contradiction. Since you, however, make your reporter's statement the basis for part of the leader in your this morning's issue, I think it is necessary to contradict the statement made by your reporter and state what actually happened. He informed me that you were most anxious to know whether the Council had been given an opportunity to consider the draft agreement and whether it had been discussed at a full Council meeting, to which the reply was in the negative. I did, however, add that on certain points Mr. Fessenden and myself had been consulted. As a matter of fact, at the first meeting of the foreign delegates which I, as Chairman of the Council, was asked to attend, I was informed that their instructions were only to consult me. I stated that any opinion that I might give would be of little value unless supported by someone with experience of the inner workings of the Court. I asked to be allowed to request Mr. Fessenden, the Director General of the Council who had had over twenty-five years' experience in the working of the Mixed and Provisional Courts, by telephone, to attend the meeting. As a result of this, Mr. Fessenden attended this and the three subsequent meetings which were held, but which we were requested to consider as being absolutely confidential. I am neither approving nor disapproving of the attitude of the Diplomatic Body in dealing with this matter, but in order not to mislead the public, I wish to point out that even if the draft agreement had been discussed at a full Council meeting, the Council would largely have been guided by the views of the Director General, in view of his long experience of the working of the Mixed and Provisional Courts.

We were not requested to state what the Council desired, but were informed that certain provisions in the present agreement would not be accepted by the Chinese and we were asked to make such practical suggestions as might occur to us which might possibly be of assistance to the foreign delegates. The decision as to the practicability of any suggestions made by us was a matter resting entirely in the judgment and discretion of the foreign delegates. I would emphasize that I certainly did not say that the fact of Mr. Fessenden and myself being consulted on certain points was the same as the full Council being consulted upon the agreement as a whole, which agreement, I would repeat, was not submitted to Mr. Fessenden and myself, but that we were merely consulted on certain points.
I am, etc.,
H. E. ARNHOLD.
Shanghai, Feb. 20, 1930.

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 22, 1930

The Provisional Court

It has been complained to us by Mr. H. E. Arnhold that our article yesterday implied doubt towards the letter he had written us contradicting a statement attributed to him in our issue of January 8. We are sorry Mr. Arnhold should have read us in this sense, which was certainly not that intended. His letter taxed our reporter with a rather serious inaccuracy, and in the circumstances we think any newspaper, or any firm, would say what there was to be said in their employee's defence, the intention yesterday being to show that the misstatement was innocently made. Of course we do not doubt Mr. Arnhold's word and can only express our regret if it appeared to him that we did so. The personal question, however, and the broad issue of policy remain distinct. The methods adopted by the diplomatists all through the Provisional Court conference are as little to the taste of the public as the ultimate result, indeed even more so, since they arouse the most lively anxiety as to what may be done at any moment, with no opportunity for the foreign community to say a word in its own defence. Throughout the conference everyone who had first-hand knowledge of the workings of the Provisional Court was kept rigidly at arms length, no expert was admitted to the discussions, and we believe we are right in saying that none was ever consulted: absolute secrecy was preserved throughout. Why? There is only one possible answer, namely, that the Ministers in Peking meant to do something which they knew the foreign public of Shanghai would justly resent, and they took special precautions that nothing should leak out until it was too late for protest to avail. It is not as if there had been nothing for the Ministers to do but to cave in. There was. The terms of the British aide mémoire of December 31, which was repeated and re-emphasized after the McBride case a few days later, laid down quite clearly the stipulations and conditions under which it would alone be possible for Great Britain to meet China's wishes. This aide mémoire was in essentials an elaboration of the methods so clearly defined by Sir Austen Chamberlain at West Birmingham in January 1927, so that it would have served for guidance in the negotiations over the Provisional Court, which were not half over, when the aide mémoire arrived. There is further good ground to believe that the instructions from Washington as regards the conference would have been very acceptable to Shanghai had they been known. Finally we have the example of the French handling of their Mixed Court problem, to prove that firmness can be used and that it excites, not any "incident," but gratitude. All the circumstances of the negotiating of the new Court agreement leave an unpleasant taste and indicate a weakness that need never have been committed. But these methods will undoubtedly continue unless the Council assert themselves as a body and insist on due recognition of their enormously important position, involving not only their rights but their duties as the government of Shanghai. They can do it, and every ratepayer will back them up. But they will have to make themselves clear. They will have to use unambiguous language and be prepared to use diplomatic action.

People are beginning to complain
that our Municipal Council is secret-
ive. Such is the reward paid by
the ungrateful to those who so pat-
riotically sacrifice time, temper,
toes, and toes to the Municipal ser-
vice. Is not our "Municipal
Gazette" a standing denial to the
charge? Produced regularly once
per week, it tells in some thirty-
six columns of the numbers of beans
estimated to be eaten by convicts in
the Municipal Gaol during the ensu-
ing so much, and for which beaners
or would-bes are invited to tender.
Also, boots, Sikh, large, very:
spectacles, sun, tinted according to
rank: and so forth.
Also, does it not set forth:—
At the meeting of the Works
Committee held on Tuesday, January
21, 1930, at 5 p.m., there are present:
Messrs. (several of them). The
Minutes of the last meeting are con-
firmed and signed. The meeting
terminates at 6.45 p.m."
After all, one is compelled to
think of the gentleman who put off
from a dock side in a dinghy, had
himself rowed out to a smart battle-
cruiser and said he had come to
look over it. Informed by the
officer of the watch that it was not
a visiting day, he proclaimed in-
dignantly that he was a taxpayer,
that he had helped to build that
battle-cruiser and that he intended
at least to see his money's worth.
Whereupon, the officer twisted off
a nut from a stanchion, handed it
to the visitor and said:—"There
you are, old bean! There's the bit
you bought. Take it and keep it,
and don't come making dirty foot-
marks on what other people have
bought. They might not like it, you
know!"
Thinking it over, is there any
ratepayer, paying his rates, who
will contend that he does not get
his money's worth when he gets
thirty-six of those columns fifty-two
times a year—a week's labour for
each set of thirty-six—and an addi-
tional thirty-six or more produced
by a professional journalist in six
hours once a year after Ratepayers
Meetings, thrown in for no extra
rates?
But there is another side to it
which the average ratepayer does
not understand, because he does not
have to do with it. The Municipal
Council is not secretive: there is no
body on this earth from whom it is
easier for one to get information,
if he is in perfect physical condi-
tion and is tenacious of life. Shang-
hai has just seen "Charley's Aunt"
and getting information out of the
Municipal Council is just as easy as
getting that half-crown out of
Brassett. For instance, one is in-
structed to inquire of the Municipal
Council, or its component parts,
why it is that certain very plainly
printed, signed, dated, and witness-
ed rules applying to the tramway
and omnibus companies are broken
unchallenged every inch of every
journey made by every tram and
bus.

One embarks hopefully on the
quest, because obviously, if there
are such rules—and there are—and
if there is an official of the Muni-
cipal Council specially designated as
being in charge of "information"—
as there is—why, the job's easy.
The disappointment is prompt and
complete. He would be delighted
to save one any trouble if he had
the information to give, but that is
the sort of thing regarding which
one should inquire in the Secret-
ariat. So, to the Secretariat, who
would be only too pleased to supply
full particulars, but it seems to be
more a case for the Director-Gener-
al. The Director-General sees no
reason whatever why full publicity
should not be given to the matter:
in fact, when he was Chairman, he
had no hesitation in authorizing the
circulation of the fullest details re-
garding such matters. But then,
you know, one cannot say off-hand
what the Chairman might think of
it. Thence to the Chairman, who is
in complete accord with the desire
that the public should be made fully
acquainted with the facts, but, after
all, he cannot be expected to carry
everything in his head, and applica-
tion should be made to the head of
the department concerned.
The head of department is always

which his department has cognis-
ance, but then, you know, nothing
can be given out except with the

fully and reports that neither the

pany ever break any rules, that it

four.

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, WEDNESDAY, MARCH 19, 1930.

Provisional Court Changes
Meet With Criticism

General Chamber Of Commerce Deprecates Decision
To Hand Control To Chinese; Members
Hear Review Of Past Year

At the annual general meeting of the General Chamber of Commerce held yesterday afternoon, the acting-Chairman, Mr. H. W. P. McMeekin, in the absence of Mr. V. G. Lyman, Chairman, gave members an outline of the activities of the Chamber during the past year. In addressing the meeting he said:

I am occupying the chair at this meeting in the unavoidable absence of our Chairman, Mr. V. G. Lyman, who I am sorry to say had a nervous breakdown some weeks ago and the Chamber has been deprived of his valued services as a member of the committee and Chairman of the Chamber. Mr. Lyman has been a member of the committee of the Chamber for the last six years, during which time he served as Vice-Chairman for three years and was elected chairman at the last annual general meeting. In wishing Mr. Lyman a speedy restoration to good health, I am sure I am expressing the wish of all members of the Chamber.

The report and accounts have been in your hands for some time and with your permission I will take them as read. I will ask you to adopt them in due course.

Perusal of the report gives an indication of the many matters which have called for your Committee's attention during the year.

Your Chairman referred in his remarks last year to the Amherst Rocks and the wireless beacon which was to be installed there by the Chinese Government. The Chamber has recently received a communication from the Coast Inspector which states that a radio beacon has been erected at the North Saddle and has already been in operation for several months. The main object of this aid is to enable ships to get a line of bearing during fog and in clear weather, and so enable them to avoid Amherst Rock.

Accuracy Obtained

According to the Coast Inspector, although this radio beacon is still considered to be in the experimental stage, it has been favourably commented upon, bearings having been taken at distances of over 100 miles with very considerable accuracy. It is understood that if on further trial this beacon continues to give satisfaction it is the intention of the Coast Inspector to recommend the establishment of certain similar aids and the next to be erected will probably be established at Shaweishan Light Station, if it is decided that the location is satisfactory. With two radio beacons, a ship, according to the Coast Inspector, should be able to get a fix, with cross bearings from the beacons, sufficiently accurate to clear Amherst Rock.

The question of pilotage has been constantly before your committee during the year. The Woosung-Hankow Pilotage Association made preliminary representations for an increase in their tariff of charges, but after consulting interested parties the Chamber replied that shipping companies would not consent to any increase in the tariff at this juncture, the general view being that the difficulties complained of by the pilots should be met by a complete reorganization of the service, which latter appears to be inevitable.

Guarding Pilotage

Shipping companies have also given notice of the fact that the existing tariff of the Shanghai Licensed Pilots' Association comes up for revision after June 30, next, and they intend to demand a considerable reduction in same. The matter is at present in the hands of the Pilotage Authority and nothing more can be said on the subject for the present, but if past experience is to be taken as an indication, the Chamber will have a difficult question to deal with, requiring the most careful handling.

The Chamber is not unmindful of the excellent services which are being maintained by the existing pilotage organizations, and anything which is calculated to reduce the efficiency of those services must be strongly deprecated and guarded against at all costs. The peculiarities of the approaches to Shanghai and the tortuous channel in the harbour cannot be lost sight of, but on the other hand, shipping companies complain of the heavy burden which the present tariff of the Shanghai Licensed Pilots' Association, inflated during the lean years of the Great War, imposes.

Emphatic Protest

Matters connected with the Shanghai Provisional Court have on many occasions in the past occupied the attention of this Chamber and I should like at this juncture to put on record that we strongly deprecate the arbitrary manner in which the negotiations have been completed regarding the proposed closing of the Court as from April 1, 1930, and the inauguration in its place of Chinese Courts.

The fact that neither the Shanghai Municipal Council nor commercial interests were consulted during the conferences held between the Chinese authorities and the Ministers of the foreign Powers must be viewed with grave concern by all foreigners and Chinese having the future safety and prosperity of Shanghai at heart.

In expressing these sentiments, let it be clearly understood that this Chamber is not prepared to support any movement or action calculated to prevent or unnecessarily delay China from attaining her natural aspirations, including full sovereignty, but any undue hastening of the process without proper safeguards must bring disaster on all concerned.

During the year under review we have experienced a steady decline in the price of silver and our T. T. rate has fallen in sympathy from 2/7¼ on January 3, 1929 to 2/1 on December 31, 1929. Since the close of the year further sharp declines have taken place, the lowest official quotation being 1/10 T. T. per tael on the 5th of the present month. This figure has eclipsed all previous low levels, such as 2/1½ in 1902 and 2/1¾ in 1914.

This severe decline in the purchasing value of our local currency has naturally reacted adversely on importers in general and particularly those who sell to native merchants on a sterling basis. Many of the latter, through not having fixed exchange, have been unable to meet their sterling commitments and the onus of loss has devolved on the foreign importers. This has been particularly heavy in the textile trade and this Chamber has just recently sponsored a movement approved by the national chambers for the formation of a Piece Goods Association having as one of its chief objectives, the standardization of sales in local currency.

MR. ARNHOLD EXPLAINS HIS RESIGNATION
Editor,
THE SHANGHAI TIMES
Sir.—May I through your columns thank the 715 electors of this community, representing more than half the votes recorded, who voted for me for their support at the recent election and explain the reason for my resignation of the Chairmanship of the Council before termination of my period of office?
In view of the leading article in one of your contemporaries this morning and the reference to the controlling interest of the Japanese voters in the ultimate result, I feel it incumbent upon me to bring certain facts to the attention of the ratepayers, which it is in their interests to know.
As Chairman of the Council I have been unable to agree to certain requests which have been pressed upon me for what appeared to be a disproportionate increase in the Japanese police and other matters, which could not be granted in their entirety. As a result of this, I was given to understand a few days prior to the election that I should only receive 209 out of the 609 Japanese votes. If this actually occurred, the foreign community must have supported me to the extent of 515 votes.
I understand that 90 per cent. of the Japanese electorate went to the poll, as compared with about 50 per cent. of the British. It is, therefore, evident that so long as the British community do not turn out in larger numbers to cast their vote, Municipal affairs will be controlled by the Japanese voting machine. Possibly, the community may show more interest in Municipal affairs now that "new blood" has been infused into the Council "to shake it up."
May I, in this connection, remind you that a similar hope was expressed in the Press at the time of my election to the Council two years ago? The chief object for which I was asked to stand was to secure the carrying out of the recommendations of the Economy Committee. During the year of my tenure of office as Chairman the following has, in that respect, been achieved:—
1.—The Municipal Hospitals and Nursing system have been reorganized, resulting in greater efficiency and economy.
2.—The Commissioner of Police has resigned and the services of a highly qualified police executive obtained from India to reorganize the Police Force, the reorganization of which is now nearly completed.
3.—Schemes have been evolved for the housing and improve-

telephone service, pointing out that the Telephone Company had broken the terms of its franchise.
I felt very strongly that in view of the Council's grave responsibility to the public in this respect, it was imperative that the Council should obtain the services of an independent expert. The Telephone Company and the Council's nominee on the Board of Directors of that Company opposed this proposal on the ground that the expert's advice would serve no useful purpose, as the Company was committed to its present system. Mr. B. C. There is a lull in the storm caused by this year's surprise election for Municipal honors, and no further developments have taken place. The vacancy for chairmanship of the retiring council is being filled by Brig.-General E. B. Macnaghten, the vice-chairman, who will occupy this post until after the annual meeting of ratepayers which is to take place April 16.

In connection with his resignation at the special council meeting called last Wednesday evening, Mr. H. E. Arnhold has sent us the following letter for publication:

Editor, THE CHINA PRESS

Sir:—May I through your columns thank the 715 electors of this Community, representing more than half the votes recorded, who voted for me, for their support at the recent election and explain the reason for my resignation of the Chairmanship of the Council before termination of my period of office?

In view of the Leading Article in one of your contemporaries this morning and the reference to the controlling interest of the Japanese voters in the ultimate result, I feel it incumbent upon me to bring certain facts to the attention of the ratepayers, which it is in their interests to know.

As Chairman of the Council I have been unable to agree to certain requests which have been pressed upon me for what appeared to be a disproportionate increase in the Japanese Police and other matters, which could not be granted in their entirety. As a result of this, I was given to understand a few days prior to the election that I should only receive 200 out of the 600 Japanese votes. If this actually occurred, the Foreign Community must have supported me to the extent of 515 votes.

I understand that 90% of the Japanese electorate went to the Poll, as compared with about 50% of the British. It is therefore evident that so long as the British Community do not turn out in larger numbers to cast their vote, Municipal affairs will be controlled by the Japanese voting machine. Possibly, the Community may show more interest in Municipal affairs now that "new blood" has been infused into the Council "to shake it up."

May I, in this connection, remind you that a similar hope was expressed in the Press at the time of my election to the Council two years ago? The chief object for which I was asked to stand was to secure the carrying out of the recommendations of the Economy Committee. During the year of my tenure of office as Chairman, the following has, in that respect, been achieved:—

1. The Municipal Hospitals and Nursing System have been reorganized, resulting in greater efficiency and economy.

2. The Commissioner of Police has resigned and the services of a highly qualified police executive obtained from India to reorganise the Police Force, the reorganisation of which is now nearly completed.

3. Schemes have been evolved for the housing and improvement in the living conditions of both the Foreign and Chinese Police Force.

4. The Department of the Director of Chinese studies has been completely reorganized under a new and efficient hand, and the old system, which was found to be wasteful, has been discarded.

5. A Staff reorganization has been set in motion, with a view to cutting out dead wood in order to give more encouragement to the more promising junior members of the Staff, to encourage efficiency and at the same time to effect economies; the results of this reorganisation may not be apparent to the public for a little time.

6. Steps have been taken gradually to make way for the greater employment of capable Chinese in the Municipal service.

7. A Salaries Commission has been appointed and is now sitting to go into the question of Salaries generally and make recommendations to the Council.

8. A Staff Association has been formed, with a view to harmonizing the relations between the Council and the Staff.

9. The whole of the Council's Educational System is in process of reorganization to provide for the equal distribution of the Council's educational facilities between the Foreign and Chinese Communities, thus removing a great source of grievance to the Chinese population of the Settlement. This reorganization, whilst effecting very considerable economy and giving direction to the Council's educational policy, will not only effect economies but will increase the efficiency of the schools, which are now being placed under a permanent Board of Education in conjunction with a Supervisor of Schools.

There is a great deal more to be done to complete all this work, but I can leave it to the public to decide whether the mandate, which I was given, has been persistently carried out, or not.

Chinese Ratepayers Assn. and

PUBLICATION OF TEXT
DEMANDED

Agitation is going on in local
Chinese circles against the new
agreement regarding the reorgan-
ization of the Shanghai Provisional
Court. On Thursday, the Chinese
Ratepayers Association and the
Amalgamated Street Unions sent
telegrams to the National Govern-
ment, expressing opposition to cer-
tain supposed provisions of the new
agreement and demanding publica-
tion of the full text without delay
so as to clear away misunderstand-
ings.

The Chinese Ratepayers Associa-
tion, in their wire, say:—
“According to the ‘Shanghai
Evening Post,’ the new agreement
recently concluded at the Provision-
al Court Reorganization Conference
stipulates that all cases involving
people who have violated the
Municipal By-laws will be dealt with
by the various Police Stations unless
the fine involved is $50 or more,
when such persons will be sent to
the reorganized Provisional Court
for trial.
“The public are amazed over this
statement and question its veracity.
The purpose of reorganizing the
Provisional Court was to bring
about the unification of China’s
judicial system and to make pre-
parations for the abolition of joint
hearing system and executive rights
of Consular Deputies in the Court.
“Whether the joint hearing system
is to be abolished in the Court is
not known to us because the new
agreement has not yet been publish-
ed. But attention should be drawn
to the fact that people who violated
the police regulations of the Inter-
national Settlement of Shanghai in
the past have been tried by the
Provisional Court even though the
fine involved only $1.
“If the ‘Evening Post’ report is
correct, then the power of the
Shanghai Municipal Police, instead
of being limited, will be greatly in-
creased because the police, being
vested with the right of imposing
fines, will arrest, detain and fine
residents at their own discretion.
This is a violation of world-
recognized judicial independence and
an encroachment upon the people’s
legal privileges. The Association
must, therefore, request you to re-
consider this question and to rectify
the errors because the residents of
Shanghai are greatly surprised by
the report appearing in the ‘Shang-
hai Evening Post’.”

Council and Agreement
Interviewed yesterday on the sub-
ject of the Provisional Court Agree-
ment, Mr. H. E. Arnhold, Chair-
man of the Shanghai Municipal
Council, stated that the agreement
had not been the subject of any
Council meeting. He himself and
Mr. Fessenden, Director of the
International Settlement, had been
consulted, which he said amounted to
the same thing as the Council taking
part in the negotiations.
Asked whether the terms obtain-
ed might have been worse, he re-
plied in the affirmative. Asked
whether they might have been
better, he answered “Of course: any-
thing can be better than it is. A
compromise of any sort is bound to
be unsatisfactory to both parties.”

According to the Min Kuo Pao,
vernacular paper published in Nan-
king, the text of the new agree-
ment concerning the reorganiza-
tion of the Shanghai Provisional
Court is as follows:

(1) The reorganization of the
Shanghai Provisional Court is to
make the tribunal a district court
conforming to the judicial system
of China.

(2) The Kiangsu Higher Court
is to be the appeal court for the
tribunal and the higher, and final
court for appeal will be the Nan-
king Supreme Court.

Prosecution And Jails.

(3) A prosecutors' office is to be
established in the tribunal for pro-
secuting criminals. The power
to arrest and detain the prisone-
rs is in the hands of the Minis-
try of Justice.

(4) Detention and judicial police
are to be established in the court
to execute the decisions of the tri-
bunal.

(5) The registrars and judicial
police will function under the direct
supervision and supervision of
the court. The court also has the
power to dismiss and appoint the
registrars and members of the
judicial police.

Examination Of Judges.

(6) All judges and prosecutors
are to be Chinese citizens, and
must have passed the examina-
tion for judges and prosecutors
held by the Ministry of Justice.

(7) The chief judge and the pros-
ecutor are to be appointed by the
National Government upon the
recommendation of the Ministry
of Justice. Other judges and pros-
ecutors are to be appointed by
the Ministry of Justice.

(8) The salaries of the judges
and prosecutors are to be fixed
by the Ministry of Justice.

(9) The court is to have a seal
which is to be used on all official
documents.

Further Provisions For
(1) Foreign lawyers will be
admitted to practice in the court
provided they have obtained certi-
ficates from the Ministry
of Justice which are to
be issued according to the Chinese
laws governing legal practitioners.
They are to apply Chinese law only.

(2) The police shall produce the
prisoners who are desired by the
court to be summoned or arrested
without delay. Other authorities
other than the police should obtain
special permission from the Court
before arresting and handing over
prisoners.

(10) The agreement is to be
effective for three years from the
date of signature by both parties.
This agreement may be amended
by mutual consent during the three
years, and may continue to be
effective after expiration on agree-
ment of both parties.

There also are three addenda to
the Provisional Court agreement.

Release of the text of the recent-
ly negotiated Provisional Court
Agreement has been delayed as the
representatives of the powers who
conducted the negotiations with of-
ficials of the Nanking Government,
have not received as yet acceptance
of the terms from the legations in
Peking. Release of the agreement
followed some weeks ago when
negotiations had been held up.

CHINESE COURTS IN
SHANGHAI

The publication of the actual terms of the agreement which sets up three Chinese courts in the International Settlement in place of the old Provisional Court reveals no great novelty for those who have been following events. It only confirms their forebodings, born of the various anticipations of the agreement which have been published in the past week or two. Frankly, it must be said that the agreement conveys the impression of having been concluded, on the foreign side, by men who had no first-hand knowledge of the Provisional Court and took no advice from those who had. And this in fact appears to have been the case. The Council were never given an opportunity to consider the draft. We know this from a recent statement by the Chairman, Mr. H. E. Arnhold, who added that he himself and Mr. Fessenden, the Director General, had been consulted, "which amounted to the same thing as the Council taking part in the negotiations." With all courtesy we must emphatically point out that it is not the same thing. We feel constrained to recall that Mr. Fessenden, though undoubtedly a valuable servant of the community, is still its servant and not a Municipal Councillor; and while we have great respect for Mr. Arnhold's ability, in a matter so serious as that of the fate of the Provisional Court his opinion cannot be admitted as representing more than his personal views. We regret to have to speak thus plainly. But the Councillors generally owe it to the ratepayers to see that what has occurred in this instance does not become a precedent. The diplomatists concerned in the signing of the new agreement were enabled to report, and have no doubt reported, to their respective Governments that the Council have acquiesced in the scheme, and it is necessary to point out that the Council as such never saw it before its publication to the world. As for the Deputies, there is, what we can only call, a most unjust tendency in some quarters to imply that they were principally responsible for the troubles in the Provisional Court. That indignation may have occasionally carried them beyond the bounds of policy, is conceivable. But those who know what their experiences were prefer to think of the Deputies as conscientious men, with a clear duty to perform, who could not keep silence before the abuses they saw. Of which indeed there was no lack.

Under the new scheme there will be no Deputies, and one may faintly wonder whether their official superiors will, in the upshot, have any the easier time for being relieved of their protest. Chinese judges will sit alone and it will only be possible in certain cases for the Council to be represented by a lawyer "who may submit to the Court his views in writing during the proceedings and who may, if he deems necessary, file a petition in intervention in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure." The normal result of such representations can but too easily be imagined. One cannot but contrast the method followed in respect of the French Mixed Court, wherein the authorities of the Concession, plainly stating that they are the people responsible for the peace and order of the Concession, reserve the right to put an Assessor on the Bench when they think necessary. And for the changes actually vouchsafed, the Chinese officials have publicly expressed their pleasure and thanks. There is no apparent reason why the foreign Ministers in whose hands lay the fate of the Provisional Court should not have followed the same course in these turbulent and uncertain times. Lest it should be thought that we take too gloomy a view, let us add that we do not doubt the good faith of Dr. C. T. Wang with whom the agreement was concluded or of the President of the Judicial Yuan, under whose department the new Courts will come. Dr. Wang Chung-hui's reputation stands deservedly high and we are sure that he is as keen as anyone can be that the new Courts should be a success. But it is impossible to be blind to the fact that the Chinese Ministers with whom agreements are made are not the men with whom the ultimate power rests. The whole system of government exposes their rules to revision by some indeterminate authority in the background and opens the door to intrigue and obstruction. And what would be the Settlement's position if Nanking's enemies or local wave of Communism, say, succeeded in overthrowing them? We hope that will not happen, but it is a contingency which ought not to be overlooked by those who are supposed to care for foreign, and Chinese, interests in Shanghai.

There is proverbially no use in crying over spilt milk. It may have dwelt upon the manifold weakness of the new agreement and particularly on the not easily defensible methods by which it was reached, it is in order that we may show up in stronger relief the solitary safeguard it offers for the Council as the body responsible for the peace of Shanghai, and the vital importance of ensuring that that safeguard shall be made operative to the fullest possible extent. Article VI provides that the Council shall supply the men who are to form the judicial police of the Courts; and it is further agreed that the Council shall designate an officer "to whom will be allotted by the President an office on the Court premises and who will make an entry of all judicial processes of the Courts, such as summonses, warrants, orders and judgments, for the purpose of service or execution". No time should be lost by the Council in deciding what it can and will do under these provisions and in making known its intentions with no uncertain voice. Let us recall what happened at the beginning of 1927, when the old Mixed Court gave place to the Provisional. No preparations had been made on the foreign side; no foreigner connected with the Court from the Deputies downwards knew what his place was: the result was all sorts of pretensions on the Chinese side, a general confusion which might have degenerated into something much worse. With far greater changes in prospect on April 1, the Council must be prepared and they cannot begin their preparation too soon. This is not a departmental matter, but a vital question for the whole Council with the assistance of all the advice of those on whom will lie the duty of carrying out their decisions, and it is not to be ignored that the Council will have to make up their mind to speak plainly, to leave no doubt that they will act firmly, and that they will not be content with mere diplomatic assurances. They are the Government of Shanghai, with whom rests the supreme duty of keeping law and order in the Settlement and they can count on the unanimous support of ratepayers in making it perfectly clear that they will fulfil that duty no matter at what cost. We sincerely hope and would fain believe that the new agreement will work smoothly. But the times are too critical to allow any misplaced delicacy or waste of time in taking such precautions against mishap as that Agreement permits.

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 26, 1930

COUNCIL AND
POWERS

The implication of recent articles, as readers will readily have seen, is that the Municipal Council must assert itself and take a determined line where its duty calls and its rights are at stake. In some quarters this seems to have been taken to mean that the Council generally should defy the Powers, suggesting that Shanghai intends to manage its own business and would be glad to see them manage theirs. This is surely an irrational, exaggerated interpretation of a quite reasonable principle, the easy refuge of those who only seek the line of least resistance. Because the Powers have declared their readiness to meet China's wishes as and when it may be feasible to do so, it does not follow that they are merely competing with each other to see who can throw everything away first, and it is a bad mistake to assume that this is their resolve, and consequently that there is nothing for us in Shanghai to do but to sit with folded hands and await our doom.

Three important facts should be borne in mind in this connection. First, let us again quote from the British aide-mémoire handed to the Nanking Government at the close of last December. The concluding sentence reads as follows:

His Majesty's Government are ready to enter into detailed negotiations, as soon as political conditions in China render it possible to do so, with a view to agreeing on a method and a programme for carrying abolition of extraterritoriality into effect by gradual and progressive stages to the mutual satisfaction of both governments.

It may safely be assumed that other Powers would, on the whole, endorse this attitude; certainly they would not proceed more quickly; probably they would be even more cautious. But the passages we have italicized show conclusively that the Foreign Office does not lose sight of certain clear safeguards and stipulations which must be fulfilled before it can meet Chinese wishes in full. From Shanghai's point of view this statement is of the greatest importance. Shanghai itself is the very core of the whole question of extraterritoriality. Any measures tending towards the removal of consular jurisdiction must strike at the independence of Shanghai. If, then, a Minister is found exceeding the pace set by his own government, or interfering in negotiations which affect Shanghai as a whole without the knowledge and consent of his colleagues in Peking, the Council have every right to take exception to his conduct and to shape their own course, regardless of any attempt at dictation by him.

The second fact which may justly be stressed is that the Council are the only government of Shanghai, responsible for the maintenance of law and order and the protection of its interests, both Chinese and foreign, until the situation under which it has always functioned is reversed. Wild and gloomy statements have been repeated to us that "the Powers could wipe out Shanghai with a stroke of the pen." There is no doubt they could do so. There is equally no doubt that they would never dream of doing so. It is an old saying that "circumstances alter cases." What the Powers might possibly have felt justified in doing as regards Shanghai even fifty years ago would be at once recognized as quite inadmissible today, when Shanghai has become one of the largest and most important cities in the world. If the Council could show reasonable cause for any line of action they felt bound to take, the Powers would never repudiate them, and we may further be confident that they would not disregard the Council's wishes if these were firmly enough expressed. If the Council's representations on certain matters have, in the past, been rejected in London or Washington, that was not because they were unreasonable or inequitable, but simply because the demand was not pressed with sufficient resolution.

And the third fact to be remembered is the appointment of Judge Feetham. He has been brought here to study the history and problems of Shanghai and to advise on its future constitution conformably with the satisfaction of Chinese wishes and the protection of Chinese and foreign business interests. It has been made known unofficially that the principal Powers welcomed Judge Feetham's appointment and will be pleased to consider the scheme he may suggest for the solution of a problem which no one yet has attempted to solve. The obvious corollary of this attitude is that the Powers shall wait, before making any changes liable to affect Shanghai, until Judge Feetham has finished his work. By calling him to do that work at its own expense, the foreign community of Shanghai has given unequivocal proof that it accepts the principle that changes are in store, and is doing its utmost to assist in their execution. This fact gives it the right to ask that the scope of Judge Feetham's inquiry shall not be capriciously restricted or the ground cut from under his feet. By the fact alone of having called in such an advisor, the Council are put in an unassailably strong position to insist that, while they still remain the government of Shanghai, they shall not be hampered in the execution of their duty.

It may further be emphasized that the Council is one, a continuous, unchanged government, based on many decades of tradition, custom, precedent, and wide experience. The Diplomatic Body, for practical purposes, is too often only an expression: actually, it is composed of sixteen or seventeen men liable to pull in as many different directions, always subject to orders from political parties thousands of miles away whose views are perpetually influenced by the wish to catch and retain votes at home; and these men, sent out here for a few years to represent their respective governments, would be more than human if their principal preoccupation were not to avoid doing anything which might endanger their chances of a better post when they are moved on from China. In all complicated questions the man who makes up his mind to a given line of action and follows it without fear or favour is the one most sure of success. It is a maxim which the Council may be urged to keep clearly before their eyes. The fear that the Powers would throw us down or repudiate us is, frankly, rubbish. The Council have not been given to acting without reason and reflection in the past, and they are not likely to do so at any time. More than once in recent years we have heard from London that it was impossible for the British Government to understand what Shanghai really wanted, so many and different were the opinions uttered by Shanghai men. That is the Council's opportunity, to take the lead conformably with the facts set out above and to keep it resolutely.

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 19, 1930.

Text Of New Provisional
Court Agreement Issued;
Goes Into Effect April 1

Deputy System Is Abolished In Re-organized Court;
Ministries At Nanking Consider Question Of New Personnel

Following the signing at Nanking on Monday of the agreement relative to the re-organization of the Shanghai Provisional Court, a meeting of the ranking members of the Ministry of Judicial Administration including Minister Wei Tao-ming and Counsellors Wu and Chien Tai, was held under the chairmanship of President Wang Chung-hui of the Judicial Yuan to decide, upon the re-organization measures to be adopted for the Court.

It is understood that in order to carry out the efficient administration of justice by the new tribunal the candidates for the Presidency and Judgeships of the Court will be subject to careful examination by the judicial officer selection and examination committee of the Ministry of Judicial Administration before being recommended to the Government for appointment.

Actual re-organization of the Court, it is said, will be effected at the latest by April 1 of the current year.

In regard to the question of foreign lawyers practising in the new Court, it is reliably learned that they will be allowed to appear as counsel provided that they possess certificates from their respective consulates according to the rules of the bar and its immediate jurisdiction, the Branch High Court of Kiangsu being the only one in the following:

1.—When both litigants are foreigners.
2.—When the Shanghai Municipal Council is complainant in a civil or criminal action and
3.—When the Shanghai Municipal Council is prosecutor.
Kuo Ming.

The full text of the agreement follows:

From the date on which the present Agreement comes into force, all laws, regulations, judgments, and decisions having effect prior to the establishment of the Courts in the International Settlement at Shanghai shall be abolished.

Article II

The Chinese Government shall in accordance with Chinese laws and regulations relating to the judiciary and subject to the terms of the present Agreement, establish in the International Settlement at Shanghai a District Court (Ti Fang Fa Yuan) and a Branch High Court (Kao Teng Fa Yuan Fen Yuan). All Chinese laws and regulations, substantive as well as procedural, which are now in force, or which may hereafter be duly enacted and promulgated shall be applicable in the courts, due account being taken of the Land Regulations and Bye-laws of the International Settlement, which are applicable pending their adoption and promulgation by the Chinese Government, and of the terms of the present Agreement.

Judgments, decisions and rulings of the Branch High Court are subject to appeal, according to Chinese law, to the Supreme Court of China.

Article III

The former practice of consular deputies or consular officials appearing to watch proceedings, or to sit jointly in the Chinese Court now functioning in the International Settlement shall be discontinued in the Courts established under the present Agreement.

Article IV
